label: Convergence of metric-measure spaces
notes: Chapter 27 occupies printed pages 743 to 772 and asks what it means for one whole geometry to approach another. We package distance and mass into a single metric-measure space and then build topologies on the collection of all such spaces, so that curvature bounds survive a limiting process.

label: What is a metric-measure space
notes: A metric-measure space bundles a complete separable metric with a reference probability measure of full support. Normalizing the total mass to one removes a scaling ambiguity, and treating isomorphic spaces as identical means we compare shapes, not labelings, which is exactly what a convergence theory for geometries must do.

label: Why we need a topology on spaces
notes: Synthetic Ricci bounds are stated for fixed spaces, yet their value lies in stability. If a sequence of spaces with a common lower bound converges, the limit should inherit the bound. To make sense of that sentence we first need a precise topology in which the sequence converges at all.

label: Gromov-Hausdorff distance
notes: The Gromov-Hausdorff distance measures geometry without coordinates. We embed two spaces isometrically into a common host and take the Hausdorff distance of their images, then minimize over all embeddings. Equivalently we look for an approximate isometry, a correspondence that distorts pairwise distances by at most a small amount.

label: Measured Gromov-Hausdorff topology
notes: The measured version asks for more than near-isometry of the supports. The approximate isometry must also push the reference measure of one space close to that of the other in a weak sense. Mass and metric move together, so densities cannot quietly escape to infinity while the shapes appear to match.

label: Correspondences and approximate isometries
notes: A correspondence is a relation pairing points of two spaces so that every point on each side has a partner. Its distortion is the largest discrepancy between paired distances. Small distortion plus near matching of the two measures is the concrete, checkable certificate that two metric-measure spaces are close.

label: Sturm's D-distance
notes: Sturm builds an honest metric on isomorphism classes. Couple the two reference measures by a transport plan on the product, compare the two distance functions under that coupling in an L-squared sense, and minimize over couplings. This is a Gromov-Wasserstein quantity, and it makes the space of spaces itself a metric space.

label: D-distance as a Gromov-Wasserstein metric
notes: The D-distance satisfies the triangle inequality through a gluing lemma that pastes optimal couplings across three spaces. It vanishes exactly on isomorphic pairs and metrizes a topology comparable, on nice families, to the measured Gromov-Hausdorff one. We now have a genuine distance, not merely a convergence notion.

label: Precompactness theorems
notes: The payoff is compactness. A family of normalized spaces that is uniformly totally bounded, with a common diameter cap and a uniform doubling or covering control on the measures, is precompact in the D-distance. Uniform bounds therefore force convergent subsequences, the workhorse of every limiting argument.

label: Passing curvature bounds to the limit
notes: Because the entropy functionals defining curvature-dimension bounds are lower semicontinuous along measured convergence, a lower Ricci bound shared by every space in a convergent sequence transfers to the limit. The class of spaces with a fixed bound is closed, which is precisely what makes the synthetic theory robust.

label: A converging sequence, singular limit
notes: Thin tubes collapsing to a segment illustrate the phenomenon. Each thickened space is smooth, yet the measured limit is a one-dimensional interval carrying a limit density. Dimension can drop and singularities can appear, and the chapter's topology is exactly strong enough to track this collapse honestly.

label: Recap and outlook
notes: We assembled three tools: the measured Gromov-Hausdorff topology, Sturm's D-distance as a Gromov-Wasserstein metric, and precompactness under uniform bounds. Together they let curvature-dimension conditions pass to limits, closing the synthetic class and setting the stage for the stability and structure results that follow.
